This metric was adopted because it quantifies the impact for a single demand response event (in our case, each day where demand response is dispatched), but it can easily and meaningfully be 15 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications. summarized over multiple events. For example, the mean or quartile values can be used to describe how the impact changes during a year, a season, or a month. This is particularly useful when the demand flexibility impacts are later used as the input to other models seeking to represent demand flexibility but that do not endogenously represent building physics. Examples of such models include Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory’s DR-Path (Brian Gerke, 2019) and the Brattle Group’s LoadFlex model (Ryan Hledik A. F., 2019). Because the goal of this analysis is to feed results into downstream modeling efforts, we calculated the D3 metric for the aggregate load of groups of buildings of a common type located in a common geography. Figure 8 shows how the D3 metric varies with different pre-peak durations for cooling load flexibility on the hottest day of the year for each state. We used an approximate 20% reduction for the 2°F offset and an approximate 40% reduction for the 4°F offset. Although only the peak offset without any precooling can provide a significant percentage reduction, pairing that with precooling can push the reduction even further—more so in some states than others. Also, the longer the duration of precooling, the higher the percentage reduction, with the highest reduction coming from 4-hour precooling. Figure 9 shows the same metrics calculated year-round. That is, we calculated the average cooling energy consumption during the peak period for the whole year for both the baseline and the upgrade, and we calculated the difference as a percentage reduction. Some states have more percentage savings year-round than their hottest day, whereas others have less. Regardless, most show a positive correlation with the duration of the pre-peak period (at all offset levels) except for a handful of states that show a surprising negative correlation. We examined the results with the largest negative correlation—an identification with a 6°F pre-peak offset to investigate how a larger precooling duration (or having precooling at all) could result in a higher load during the peak. The answer is in how the precooling and preheating was initially implemented. In the sensitivity analysis, we always chose to either precool or preheat, depending on the daily average temperature. If the daily average temperature was less than 66°F, we classified that as a heating day, otherwise we classified the day as a cooling day; however, this might not always work neatly.
